title: NEXP versus coNEXP
formal:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), and let \(\Sigma^*\) be the set of all finite binary strings. A language is a subset of \(\Sigma^*\). Let \(\mathsf{NEXP}\) denote the languages accepted in nondeterministic time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\), with the precise uniform machine convention given below, and define \(\mathsf{coNEXP}=\{\Sigma^*\setminus L:L\in\mathsf{NEXP}\}\). Is
\[
\mathsf{NEXP}=\mathsf{coNEXP}?
\]
Equivalently, is \(\Sigma^*\setminus L\in\mathsf{NEXP}\) for every \(L\in\mathsf{NEXP}\)?
definitions:
For a binary string \(x\), let \(n=|x|\) be its length, including \(n=0\) for the empty string. A nondeterministic Turing machine has a finite program, finitely many tapes with finite alphabets, and at most two available transitions at each step. A computation branch is one sequence of those choices. The machine accepts \(x\) if at least one branch halts in its accepting state, and rejects if every branch halts in a rejecting state. All branches must halt within the stated bound, on every input. Time counts individual machine transitions, including input access and all work-tape operations.

Precisely, \(L\in\mathsf{NEXP}\) means that there exist one such machine \(M\) and positive integers \(C,k\) such that for every \(x\in\Sigma^*\), every branch of \(M\) on \(x\) halts within \(C\,2^{(n+1)^k}\) steps, and \(M\) accepts \(x\) exactly when \(x\in L\). The machine has no external oracle, advice depending on the input length, or random bits. Its program and constants are fixed before all inputs. This is the usual union of nondeterministic time classes with a polynomial in the exponent; the exponent polynomial is not fixed globally across languages.

The complement \(\overline L=\Sigma^*\setminus L\) contains exactly the strings outside \(L\), with no promise restricting the input domain. Membership in \(\mathsf{coNEXP}\) means that this complement has a machine of the kind above. The equality asks whether every language accepted within a nondeterministic exponential-time bound also has such a machine for its complement. The complement machine, its constant and its exponent may all depend on the original language and may differ from those witnessing membership in \(\mathsf{NEXP}\).

The quantifier order is \(\forall L\in\mathsf{NEXP}\;\exists(M_L,C_L,k_L)\;\forall x\in\Sigma^*\), where \(M_L\) accepts exactly \(\overline L\) and satisfies the stated branchwise time bound. No single machine deciding every language, no effective compiler from an arbitrary program to a complement program, and no preservation of the original exponent is required. The classes here are uniform classes of ordinary languages, not promise classes or circuit families.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\mathsf{NEXP}=\mathsf{coNEXP}\), or of its logical negation. A proof of equality must establish complement closure with exactly the model and quantifiers above. A proof of inequality must establish the existence of a language \(L\in\mathsf{NEXP}\) whose complement lies outside \(\mathsf{NEXP}\), excluding every uniform nondeterministic exponential-time bound for that complement.

A conditional separation, a result with an oracle or length-dependent advice, a lower bound only against a fixed exponent, or consistency of a separation with a selected formal theory does not settle the unconditional class equality. This is a yes-or-no class-comparison question, with no numerical approximation target.
why: This asks whether nondeterministic exponential-time computation is closed under exchanging yes and no answers, a basic unresolved symmetry question about the power of nondeterministic computation.

context_blocks.text: An accepting branch serves as a certificate that a string belongs to a nondeterministically accepted language. Complement closure asks whether negative answers always admit certificates within some exponential-time bound as well; the exponent may change.

The polynomial-time analogue is TCS-0002, NP versus coNP: \(\mathsf{NP}\) uses polynomial rather than exponential time, and \(\mathsf{coNP}\) consists of its complement languages. The known implication \(\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{coNP}\Rightarrow\mathsf{NEXP}=\mathsf{coNEXP}\) makes a separation here a stronger conclusion than separating NP from coNP.

TCS-7232, Asser’s problem, concerns \(\mathsf{NE}=\mathsf{coNE}\). Here \(\mathsf{NE}\) permits nondeterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\), and \(\mathsf{coNE}\) consists of its complement languages. The present card instead permits \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\), so it records the requested NEXP formulation separately.

Thapen’s 2025 paper studies consistency of the conjectured separation with specified formal arithmetic theories: whether those theories can prove the opposing inclusion. Its Theorem 2 uses the paper’s parameter-free formalization of \(\mathsf{coNEXP}\), a qualification discussed in Section 3. This result concerns what those theories can prove and does not establish an unconditional separation of the ordinary machine classes.

sentences: NEXP consists of languages accepted by a uniform nondeterministic machine in time exponential in a polynomial of the input length.
coNEXP consists of the complements of those languages.
The question is whether these two classes are equal.
A complement machine may use a different fixed polynomial in its exponent, but it receives no advice or oracle.
A complete Lean-checked proof of equality or unconditional separation is required.
